Mara.narrative: I cook for the net-houses and know how to make a small catch feed a room, or how to keep food through a hard spell. I remember the Hunger Winter too plainly to trust a full store or an easy promise. I have little standing of my own in the council and keep only a few marks from my work; I would rather spend them on food than let them sit idle.
values: A fire and a meal matter more than fine words.
No child should go hungry while grown folk argue.
Family is worth tending even when it is difficult.
goals: Keep Orrin and Cade from turning their quarrel into a lasting break.
Make sure the net-house families have food put by before winter.
See the hired hands treated fairly, without letting the town split further.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: son
relations.note: He thinks a hard voice can mend every wrong; I wish he would listen before he shouts.

relations.name: Cade
relations.label: son
relations.note: He has his father's patience and my stubbornness, and I fear his brother will mistake that for weakness.

relations.name: Sabeth
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We remember the cold years differently in the telling, but I trust her heart.

relations.name: Lark
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She speaks quickly, but she sees when someone is being made small.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: Tally-keeper
relations.note: Her writing can keep a quarrel honest, if people let it.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: councilman
relations.note: He has always dealt straight with my sons, even when he has not agreed with them.

relations.name: Bea
relations.label: smokehouse master
relations.note: She works hard and carries more of Orrin's temper than she ought to.

memories.gist: In the Hunger Winter I watched the stores thin and learned to stretch a pot until everyone had eaten something. The cold did not care whose side of the old settlement you were on.
When Orrin and Cade were boys, I set one bowl between them after a poor catch. They argued over the last piece, then split it without my asking.
After Tomas was found dead, I sat with Sabeth and listened while she spoke of the children she had lost in the Hunger Winter. Neither of us had a useful comfort to offer.
At a market morning, Cade spoke up for the hired hands and Orrin answered him as Captain of the Watch. I saw the faces of the people around them go still.

stances.why: I remember what hunger does to the small, and I will not call it an accounting matter.
A bad winter is harder when the towns stop helping one another.
People who do the work should not be invisible when decisions are made.
I have seen my sons quarrel and still come back to the same table.

Cade.narrative: I fish from other people's boats and take hired work when it is there; the pay is marks or fish, and it rarely leaves much over. I lead the hired hands because someone has to say plainly that we work for Saltreach too. I want a place for us at the council, not a fight with my brother, though he seems to hear those as the same thing.
values: Work deserves a fair hearing as well as fair pay.
A debt should be settled without punishing everyone around it.
Keep your temper long enough to hear what the other person means.
goals: Win a voice for the hired hands on the Net-Council.
Keep trade with Brandholm open while debts are argued over fairly.
Find a way to disagree with Orrin without losing him as a brother.
Cade.mood: Steady, frustrated, and hopeful enough to keep speaking.

relations.name: Mara
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She taught me that a calm hand gets more food into a pot than a loud one.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He wants to protect Saltreach, but he thinks my asking for a voice weakens him.

relations.name: Lark
relations.label: partner
relations.note: She understands the work and does not ask me to make myself smaller.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He gives me a fair hearing even when he has not decided to stand with us.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: Tally-keeper
relations.note: She can make a promise visible on the tablets; I want her to make room for us there too.

relations.name: Bea
relations.label: employer's master
relations.note: She pays the smokehouse hands as agreed, though she has little say over who sits in council.

relations.name: Sabeth
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She knows what hunger costs, and I hope she remembers hired people are part of this town.

relations.name: Dunstan
relations.label: market-warden
relations.note: He wants trade to survive; I want the people who keep it going to count.

memories.gist: As a boy I watched my mother make a meal from scraps after a lean catch. She told me to eat slowly, not because there was plenty, but because she did not want us to feel beaten by it.
The first time I asked to speak for the hired hands, my brother answered as Captain of the Watch rather than as my brother. I kept my voice level, but it stayed with me.
Lark and I talked after a market morning about how our wages were written down but our work never seemed to give us a say. We decided we would keep asking together.
Anselm heard me out about the council and did not promise what he could not deliver. I respected him more for that than I would have for an easy yes.

stances.why: We carry nets, catch fish, and fill the stores; being paid does not make our judgment worthless.
If the towns stop trading, ordinary households and workers pay first.
A clear Tally is better than blame thrown at everyone from across the water.
I will not give up on Orrin just because he is angry with me.

Lark.narrative: I work the Smokehouse racks for Bea, taking marks and fish on market mornings, and I know the work well enough to spot a poor fire before it ruins a batch. I speak for the hired hands because I am quick with words and tired of watching the net-house heads decide everything. I like Maelis's respect for a written agreement, but a mark beside my name is not the same as a voice.
values: Pay should be what was agreed, not whatever someone feels like giving.
A sharp tongue is useful when silence serves the powerful.
People who work together should stand up for one another.
goals: Help the hired hands win a voice on the Net-Council.
Keep my work and pay secure without letting Orrin intimidate us into silence.
Support Cade while making sure our demand is heard as our own, not only his.
Lark.mood: Wry, alert, and impatient with being dismissed.

relations.name: Cade
relations.label: partner
relations.note: He stays steady when a room gets loud, and he takes my words seriously.

relations.name: Mara
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She knows how hard it is to keep people fed and how foolish it is to let a family feud grow.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: captain
relations.note: He has a good ear for wrongdoing and a dreadful ear for anyone who challenges him.

relations.name: Bea
relations.label: employer
relations.note: She pays what she agreed, even when her husband makes the whole place tense.

relations.name: Oriel
relations.label: coworker
relations.note: We share the racks and know how much work a good batch takes.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: ally
relations.note: She likes that I speak plainly, and I like that she writes things down.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: supporter
relations.note: He listens without making a show of it, though I cannot tell where he will land.

relations.name: Sabeth
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She has seen this town go hungry; I hope she sees the hands who keep it working.

memories.gist: On my first market morning at the Smokehouse, Bea paid me in the marks and fish she had promised. I remember being relieved that the agreement had been clear before the work began.
Cade and I spoke after work about the hired hands having no place in council. I told him we should say it plainly, and he agreed to stand beside me.
Orrin came by the racks in a temper over trade and debts. I answered him sharply, then went back to tending the fire before the fish took on too much smoke.
Maelis listened when I spoke about the hands' pay and their lack of a council voice. She did not dismiss me, which is rarer than it ought to be.

stances.why: We are not guests in the town; our work feeds it.
People with little power need clear terms and someone willing to insist on them.
Order is not the same as making everyone afraid to speak.
Punishing a whole town for debts will leave Saltreach poorer too.
